name: 02-first-look-esp32
description: The same tree on real hardware: what a device adds that a computer cannot, from LED pins to a microphone.

steps.title: Your device
steps.caption: Your device. The same tree as on a computer, and what a device adds to it.
Every card you just saw on a computer is here too. What changes is what is behind it: this one has pins, a radio and a microphone.
Layouts: the same grid, here sixty four by sixty four. Four thousand and ninety six lights, on a device that costs a few euros.
Effects: the same Pulse you have been watching, now rendered on the chip itself.
Drivers: this is where a device differs. It has pins, so the frame can leave on a wire.
An output driver is added per device rather than built in, so here is one: the R M T driver, which clocks a strip from a single pin.
A pin, a light count, and the preset that says which channel does what. That is the whole contract between a frame and a wire.
System: the same card, now reporting the chip it runs on. Two of its parts only mean something on hardware.
I2cScan: on real hardware it finds the chips actually wired to the bus.
Pins: which pin every module has claimed, so two never fight over one.
File Manager: this is the device's own flash, so a backup here is worth taking.
Network: the WiFi it joined. Mqtt and Devices work as they do on a computer.
Services: the inputs, and on a device they read real pins.
Audio: this device has a microphone, so it is listening to the room.
Firmware: it finds the next release and installs it over the air. This one is an S3.
Behind it sits MoonBase, a second boot image that ships on the four megabyte devices. It is what brings a classic ESP32 back when an update goes wrong.
MoonCloud: the same Stats and Talk, and this device joins them with the same consent.
